references.text: Matthew's account of the temple cleansing, where Jesus found those who were selling and buying in the temple, overturned the tables of the money changers and the benches of the dove sellers ([ref:Matt 21:12-13|Matthew 21:12-13]).

Mark's account of the temple cleansing, where Jesus drove out those who were selling and buying in the temple and overturned the tables of the money changers and the benches of the dove sellers ([ref:Mark 11:15-17|Mark 11:15-17]).
Luke's account of the temple cleansing, where Jesus drove out those who were selling in the temple ([ref:Luk 19:45-46|Luke 19:45-46]).

The Mosaic law allowed Israelites to exchange their tithes for money and buy what they needed for offerings at the sanctuary ([ref:5 Mos 14:24-26|Deut 14:24-26]). This formed the background for the activities of the money changers and animal sellers in the temple.
The Mosaic law prescribed doves as an offering, which explains the presence of dove sellers in the temple ([ref:3 Mos 1:14|Lev 1:14]).

Zechariah prophesied about a day when there would no longer be any merchants in the house of the Lord, the God of hosts ([ref:Sak 14:21|Zech 14:21]). Jesus' action in the temple can be seen as a fulfillment of this prophecy.
Jeremiah accused the people of making the temple a "den of robbers" ([ref:Jer 7:11|Jer 7:11]). This accusation underlies Jesus' reaction to the commerce in the temple area.
Isaiah conveys God's promise that his house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples ([ref:Jes 56:7|Isa 56:7]). The commercial activity in the temple stood in sharp contrast to this purpose.

Malachi prophesies that the Lord will suddenly come to his temple and cleanse the sons of Levi ([ref:Mal 3:1-3|Mal 3:1-3]). Jesus' cleansing of the temple can be understood in light of this prophecy about the Messiah who purifies the temple.
